# Indigenous Peoples Day: What We Inherit, What We Reclaim, and What We Choose to Pass On


On Indigenous Peoples Day, one Blackfeet woman shares the crucial need for Indigenous education for her daughter — and her classmates.


[Sharen Kickingwoman](https://www.aclu.org/bios/sharen-kickingwoman) ,
ACLU of Montana


**Share This Page**


October 12, 2026


*Editor’s Note: Sharen Kickingwoman is a proud member of the A’aaniih and Blackfeet nations. Born and raised in Montana, she believes in enhancing tribal nations’ inherent sovereignty and that the best work for Native people is by Native people. Sharen earned her bachelor’s and master’s degrees from Stanford University, and has worked in higher education, government, and advocacy spaces. Sharen has worked with the ACLU of Montana for the past seven years, and currently serves as the advocacy, policy, and organizing director.*


As my daughter and I walked to school on her first day in kindergarten this fall, my boots about knocked off — my old school that never taught me a lick of Indian education had a tipi out front.


Cradleboard beading, including the Indigenous Justice logo for ACLU of Montana. |


ACLU of Montana


Like a lot of parents, I’ve been thinking about what her years in school will look like: the teachers she’ll remember, the friends she’ll make, the things she’ll discover about the world, and about herself. But as a Blackfeet mother, I’m also thinking about whether she will see herself in what she learns.


> “Every Montana child deserves to understand the people, histories, and cultures of the place they call home.”


When I was growing up in Missoula, Montana, the only other Native kids in my school were often my own siblings. Native people were mostly presented to us as people from the past. There wasn’t much opportunity to learn about the tribes of Montana as contemporary, living people, or to understand the richness of our histories, languages, and cultures.


I didn’t fully understand what I had missed until I left Montana for college. For the first time, I had Native peers and Native professors. I began learning history that I had never encountered in school. I remember feeling almost cheated. Why had it taken leaving Montana for me to learn things I should have been learning while growing up there?


My dad, Kevin Kickingwoman, experienced another version of that loss. He grew up in Browning, Montana on the Blackfeet Reservation. His parents spoke Blackfoot, but the language wasn’t passed down to him. He eventually set out to learn the language himself.


> “When that knowledge is missing, stereotypes and assumptions take its place.”


My dad’s path to becoming an educator wasn’t conventional. He served in the U.S. Navy, worked other jobs, and eventually found his way into teaching. When he interviewed for a job teaching Blackfoot language, he didn’t yet speak much of the language.


When they asked what he did know, he told them: “I’ll sing you any song you want.” They named a song. He sang it. They named another. He sang that one, too. Then they asked whether he wanted to learn. He did.


Today, my dad teaches the Blackfoot language, as well as the culture and history of the Blackfeet people in Browning. In 2024, he was named Montana Teacher of the Year.


> “When it is present, we have an opportunity to build understanding, respect, and connection.”


His story shows that education isn’t just about what we learn from a textbook. It is also about what one generation passes to the next, and what can happen when that chain is broken. That is one reason Indian Education for All (IEFA) matters so much to me. Montana’s Constitution recognizes the state’s unique cultural heritage and commits our schools to preserving the cultural integrity of American Indians. The Montana legislature passed IEFA in 1999 to guarantee that every public school student has the opportunity to learn about the tribal nations of the region.


The legacy of Indigenous history and culture is carried forward to the next generation. |


Sharen Kickingwoman


I am proud to work for an organization that fights to make sure those constitutional promises mean something in people’s lives. Earlier this year, the ACLU of Montana and our partners[reached a landmark settlement](https://www.aclu.org/news/racial-justice/montana-sets-gold-standard-for-indigenous-education-nationwide) with the Montana Office of Public Instruction that would create long-awaited accountability measures to help ensure our schools teach about the histories, cultures, governments, and contributions of tribal nations in Montana.


IEFA has never been just for Native kids. Every Montana child deserves to understand the people, histories, and cultures of the place they call home. When that knowledge is missing, stereotypes and assumptions take its place. When it is present, we have an opportunity to build understanding, respect, and connection.


I want my daughter to learn the things that her grandfather sought to reclaim, and that I often had to seek out for myself. I want her classmates to learn those things, too. Most of all, I hope her experience is joyful.


I hope she sees authentic representation of Indigenous people in her education. I hope she is never made to feel tokenized. I hope she feels celebrated for who she is and that her classmates grow up with a deeper understanding and respect for who we are.


My dad talks about legacy. He hopes his grandchildren will speak the language and carry forward the songs and knowledge that previous generations fought to preserve.This Indigenous Peoples’ Day, that is what I’m thinking about: what we inherit, what we reclaim, and what we choose to pass on. My daughter is just beginning her education. I hope what we pass on to her is something better.

### Rand v. State


In a case challenging New Hampshire’s school-funding scheme, the State has asked the New Hampshire Supreme Court to overturn decades of precedent recognizing a state constitutional right to an adequate education. The ACLU’s State Supreme Court Initiative, the ACLU of New Hampshire, and the National Education Association-New Hampshire filed an amicus brief urging the Court to uphold these precedents and preserve the state constitutional right to an adequate education.

### Civil Right Groups Oppose IRS Proposal That Would Politicize Tax Exempt Status to Enable Discrimination in Private Schools


WASHINGTON — Today, the American Civil Liberties Union, the Legal Defense Fund, the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, and 34 other organizations submitted a public comment in opposition to a rule proposed by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) that would allow it to revoke tax exempt status from private schools if they engage in activities the IRS unilaterally decides constitute “racial discrimination” — even if those activities are lawful. In effect, the proposed rule could undermine educational institutions’ obligation to ensure equal opportunity and freedom to teach, learn, and research by threatening to strip their tax-exempt status based on vague standards determined by the IRS alone. The comment explains that the IRS has no legal authority to unilaterally decide what constitutes racial discrimination, untethered to what the law actually prohibits. This unauthorized power grab would allow the IRS to politicize its decision-making process to impose the administration’s radical view of the law and target the president’s enemies. If implemented, the rule would go into effect in June 2027. “The IRS proposed rule could effectively re-segregate schools and open the door to more widespread discrimination. The IRS can’t trample constitutional rights when private institutions don’t fall in line with the Trump administration’s extreme political agenda,” said ReNika Moore, director of the ACLU’s Racial Justice Program. “This is not an isolated attack. It’s part of a larger pattern of the Trump administration scapegoating diversity and inclusion efforts and politicizing tax dollars.” “The IRS is attempting to seize an unprecedented power: unilateral discretion to define what counts as discrimination in the United States absent any limitations, including legality or constitutionality,” said Kellen McCoy, counsel at the Educational Opportunities Project at the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law. “And the proposed rule and this administration’s prior actions make plain that the IRS will use this authority to harm Black students and other students of color by forcing private schools to shutter lawful programs that foster equity.” “For generations, civil rights laws have helped open doors that were once closed to Black students and other historically excluded communities,” said Demetria McCain, director of policy at the Legal Defense Fund. “This proposal threatens that progress by allowing the IRS to treat lawful diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility efforts as discrimination. Private institutions shouldn’t be punished for advancing equal opportunity, and the federal government cannot rewrite the meaning of discrimination. This is a flagrant abuse of the IRS’s authority.” Because the proposed rule fails to provide a reasoned basis for the regulation or the IRS change in position, the groups urge for it to be withdrawn. An estimated 18,000 schools would be immediately affected if it is implemented. The full public comment is available here.

### Salles, et al. v. National Institutes of Health, et al.


Salles, et al. v. National Institutes of Health, et al. is a class action lawsuit challenging the censorship and termination of federally funded research by the National Institutes of Health (NIH). While ongoing litigation in APHA v. NIH successfully resulted in the reinstatement of hundreds of grants, NIH’s current policies continue to target viewpoints it opposes, threatening research because the government dislikes what it thinks the researchers believe or are likely to say, and continue to violate governing statutes and regulations. This is stymieing critical public health research, particularly related to climate change, the starkest health disparities including those faced by communities of color and LGBTQ+ populations, and other areas.


**Status:** Ongoing
